video_metadata.working_title: WASHINGTON 1972 Cold Case Solved After 48 Years — Justice for Jody Loomis
video_metadata.topic_one_sentence: In August 1972, 20-year-old Jody Loomis was shot in the woods near what is now Mill Creek, Washington, while riding her bike toward the stable where she kept her horse; a microscopic semen stain on a boot she had borrowed from her 12-year-old sister was profiled in 2008, traced by genetic genealogy in 2018 to Terrence Miller of Edmonds, who was arrested in April 2019 and found guilty of first-degree murder on November 9, 2020, hours after he took his own life.
video_metadata.primary_emotion_to_evoke: grief turning into quiet vindication: a borrowed boot and a little sister who waited 48 years to see the truth written into the court record

protagonist._instructions: The main character of your story - can be hero, villain, or antihero. Fill with verified facts only.
protagonist.full_name: Jody Gwen Loomis (victim; the story's centre). Convicted killer: Terrence (Terry) Miller of Edmonds, Washington.
protagonist.age_at_time_of_events: Jody: 20 (she had turned 20 in June 1972). Some national outlets wrongly say 19. Miller: about 30 in August 1972 (77 at his April 2019 arrest, 78 at the November 2020 verdict); ABC News reported 33, which does not fit his reported ages.
protagonist.occupation_or_status: Jody: young woman living at home with her parents, her fiance and her 12-year-old sister; horse lover. Miller (2019): retired heavy-equipment operator running a ceramics shop with his wife.
protagonist.location: Jody: single-story family home on Winesap Road, between Mill Creek and Bothell, Snohomish County, Washington. Miller: Edmonds area, about five miles from where Jody was found.
protagonist.physical_description: Not documented in the sources consulted beyond archival photos; do not describe.
protagonist.background_brief: Jody Gwen Loomis was born in 1952 and celebrated her 20th birthday in June 1972. She lived with her parents, her fiance and her younger sister Jana (12) on Winesap Road. She loved horses and kept a horse, reported as named Saudi, at a stable (reported as on Strumme Road). She also had a brother, John Loomis.
protagonist.mundane_humanizing_detail: On the day she died she was wearing a pair of St. Moritz 'waffle-stomper' boots, size 5 and a half, that she had borrowed from her 12-year-old sister Jana.
protagonist.nickname_or_alias_if_any: None documented for Jody. Miller was sometimes called Terry.

victims_or_targets._instructions: People affected by the protagonist's actions. Include 3-5 key figures minimum.

individuals.name: Jody Gwen Loomis
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Stranger to Miller; police and press said they did not know each other
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Raped and shot in the head with a .22-caliber pistol on August 23, 1972, in woods near 164th Street SW, near what is now Mill Creek
individuals.humanizing_detail: Loved horses; was riding her bicycle to the stable to ride her horse; wore her little sister's borrowed boots

individuals.name: Jana Loomis-Smith
individuals.connection_to_protagonist: Lent Jody the boots that carried the DNA
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Waited 48 years; testified at the 2020 trial and saw her old boots for the first time in 48 years
individuals.humanizing_detail: Said she did not want vengeance, only that the court record state Miller murdered her sister
individuals.any_quotes_from_them: At a bail hearing (Herald, single source): 'On that day the murderer stole Jody's life.'

individuals.name: Jody's parents
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Both died without ever learning who killed their daughter (per Jana, December 2020)
individuals.humanizing_detail: Names not confirmed in sources consulted

individuals.name: John Loomis
individuals.specific_impact_suffered: Watched the verdict by livestream; told reporters he would have preferred Miller go to prison
individuals.humanizing_detail: Single-source paraphrase; no exact quote verified

collective_victims_if_applicable.group_description: The Loomis family and the community of south Snohomish County
collective_victims_if_applicable.range_of_impacts: 48 years without an answer; two parents who died without knowing

supporting_characters._instructions: Investigators, accomplices, witnesses, family members - anyone who plays a significant role.

characters.name: Jim Scharf
characters.role_in_story: Snohomish County Sheriff's Office cold case detective, lead detective on the Loomis case
characters.key_actions_they_took: Pursued the boot DNA through genetic genealogy; same office used genealogy to make an arrest in the 1987 Jay Cook and Tanya Van Cuylenborg killings in 2018
characters.notable_quotes: On the family hearing the verdict: 'I think that was good for the (Loomis) family.' [Fox News]

characters.name: Ty Trenary
characters.notable_quotes: 'Thanks to the relentless persistence of our cold case team and new DNA technology, we are one step closer to justice for Jody.' [KOMO]

characters.name: Deb Stone
characters.role_in_story: Oregon genetic genealogist (working with Parabon NanoLabs' results)
characters.key_actions_they_took: Built family trees from GEDmatch relative matches; concluded the source was one of six sons of Jacquette and Albert Miller of Edmonds

characters.name: Parabon NanoLabs
characters.key_actions_they_took: Received the boot profile in 2018 and produced the genealogy-ready DNA data; its genetic genealogy unit was led by CeCe Moore (some reports credit Moore, most credit Deb Stone for the Loomis tree)

characters.name: Craig Matheson
characters.role_in_story: Snohomish County deputy prosecutor who tried the case
characters.key_actions_they_took: Presented the DNA case at trial in October-November 2020
characters.notable_quotes: 'It does not diminish the verdict.' Described the family's reaction as 'stoic.' [Herald]

characters.name: Laura Martin
characters.key_actions_they_took: Argued the DNA evidence was tainted and the forensic work sloppy; asked the court not to announce, then to vacate, the verdict
characters.notable_quotes: Only partial phrases reported: 'frankly no public benefit' (on announcing the verdict), 'sloppy', 'miscarriage of justice'

characters.name: Judge David Kurtz
characters.key_actions_they_took: On December 18, 2020, refused to vacate the verdict and signed a document affirming Miller's guilt had been proven beyond a reasonable doubt

characters.name: The two people who found Jody
characters.role_in_story: Young target shooters who drove up the dirt road around 5:30 p.m.
characters.key_actions_they_took: Stopped to move a tree from the road and found her
characters.notable_quotes: The man died before trial; his deposition was recorded and used

chronological_timeline._instructions: List every significant event with exact dates when possible. This is the backbone of your script.

events.what_happened: Jody Gwen Loomis is born
Terrence Miller is convicted of lewd conduct (reported also as a 1968 arrest for indecent exposure to a young girl)
events.significance: Prior record; jurors did not hear about it

events.location: Winesap Road, between Mill Creek and Bothell
events.what_happened: Jody celebrates her 20th birthday; she lives with her parents, her fiance and her 12-year-old sister

events.location: Winesap Road toward Penny Creek Road (now Mill Creek Road)
events.what_happened: Jody rides her bicycle from home toward the stable to ride her horse; she is last seen around 5 p.m. riding toward Penny Creek Road

events.location: Dirt road in woods near 164th Street SW, near what is now Mill Creek
events.what_happened: Two target shooters driving up the road stop to move a tree and find Jody, shot above her right ear with a .22-caliber pistol, wearing almost nothing but knee-high socks and dark waffle-soled boots
events.significance: Discovery within about half an hour of the last sighting

events.what_happened: Her bicycle is found discarded down an embankment
events.significance: Shows she was taken off her route

events.what_happened: The case goes cold; it becomes the county's oldest cold case; the boots are preserved in evidence
Cold case detectives send evidence from the case to the crime lab for DNA testing
Technicians report spermatozoa on one of Jody's boots (the left boot); a male profile is developed and uploaded to CODIS with no match
The profile is sent to Parabon; genealogist Deb Stone builds family trees from GEDmatch matches and concludes the source is one of six sons of Jacquette and Albert Miller of Edmonds
events.significance: Turns an anonymous profile into a family and then a short list

events.what_happened: Undercover detectives watch Terrence Miller drink coffee and recover the cup(s) he throws away
The lab confirms the DNA on the coffee cup matches the profile from the sperm on Jody's left boot
Detectives arrest Terrence Miller, 77; he is booked for first-degree murder, bail set at $1 million
The arrest is announced; Sheriff Ty Trenary credits the cold case team's 'relentless persistence'
events.significance: Public announcement; second Snohomish County cold homicide arrest using genetic genealogy

events.what_happened: Miller pleads not guilty to first-degree murder; Jana speaks at a bail hearing; bail is later lowered to $750,000
Miller posts bond and is released to live at home under private electronic home monitoring

Trial opens with statements on a Monday afternoon; prosecutors list 27 witnesses; the man who found Jody has died and his recorded deposition is used; Jana testifies and sees her boots for the first time in 48 years
Closing arguments; the defense argues the DNA evidence was tainted; jury begins deliberating (reported Friday, November 6)
Miller is found unresponsive by a family member; the medical examiner rules it a suicide (gunshot)
events.significance: He died before hearing the verdict

events.what_happened: After about two weeks of testimony, the jury finds Miller guilty of first-degree murder; the family shows no outward reaction and embraces at the recess
events.significance: Guilty verdict 48 years after the murder

events.what_happened: On what should have been sentencing day, Judge David Kurtz rejects the defense motion to vacate and signs a document affirming guilt beyond a reasonable doubt; Jana Loomis-Smith addresses the court
'Cold Case Files' airs the episode 'Woman in the Woods' about the case

cold_open_material._instructions: The most dramatic moment of your story - this will be your hook.

the_moment.exact_location: Penny Creek Road (now Mill Creek Road), between Bothell and Mill Creek, Snohomish County, Washington
the_moment.what_is_happening: A 20-year-old rides her bike toward the stable where she keeps her horse, wearing her 12-year-old sister's borrowed boots
the_moment.what_makes_it_shocking: Within about half an hour she is found shot in the woods; the man who did it leaves a microscopic stain on her left boot
the_moment.ironic_twist: The boots belonged to a 12-year-old girl who would grow up, testify at 60, and see them again for the first time in 48 years; the killer died by his own hand hours before the jury said 'guilty'.

cold_open_material.central_mystery_question: Who killed Jody Loomis, and how could a stain on a borrowed boot name him almost half a century later?

the_method._instructions: How did the protagonist do what they did? Technical details that can be explained to a general audience.
the_method.technique_name: Investigative (forensic) genetic genealogy plus discarded-object confirmation
step_by_step_explanation: 1972: the boots are collected and preserved in evidence.
2008: Washington State Patrol Crime Lab finds sperm on the left boot and develops a male DNA profile; CODIS search finds no match.
2018: the sample goes to Parabon NanoLabs, which produces genealogy-type DNA data (SNPs).
The data is compared on GEDmatch with people who had voluntarily uploaded their own DNA; distant relatives appear.
Genealogist Deb Stone builds family trees back to a couple, Jacquette and Albert Miller of Edmonds, whose six sons became the candidate pool.
Detectives focus on Terrence Miller, who had prior sex offenses and lived about five miles from the scene.
August 2018: undercover detectives retrieve a coffee cup he discarded at the Tulalip Resort Casino.
The state crime lab matches the cup DNA to the boot profile; arrest April 10, 2019.
the_method.why_it_worked: The stain on the boot had been preserved for 46 years, and by 2018 enough ordinary people had uploaded DNA to GEDmatch for distant cousins to point to one family.

technical_terms_to_explain.simple_explanation: The FBI-run database of DNA profiles from offenders and crime scenes; it only finds people already in it.
A much larger read-out of DNA letters, the kind consumer ancestry tests use, that can find distant cousins.
A free website where people upload their own DNA results to find relatives; launched in 2010.
DNA collected from something a person throws away in public, like a coffee cup, used to confirm or rule out a match.

the_method.scale_of_operation: Six brothers in one family; one coffee cup; one stain.

systemic_failure._instructions: What institution, system, or authority failed to prevent this?
systemic_failure.institution_that_failed: Not a failure of misconduct so much as of time and technology: 1972 forensics could not read the stain; 2008 CODIS had no matching profile.
systemic_failure.why_they_failed: DNA technology did not exist in 1972; Miller was not in CODIS in 2008 despite a 1968 lewd conduct conviction (pre-DNA-database era)
specific_incompetence_examples: No documented misconduct found; defense alleged sloppy forensic handling of the boots, which the jury did not accept
systemic_failure.ironic_details_about_the_failure: The evidence that solved the case sat in storage the whole time; the killer lived about five miles away; Jody's parents both died without knowing.

the_investigation.investigating_agency: Snohomish County Sheriff's Office (cold case unit), Washington State Patrol Crime Lab, Parabon NanoLabs
the_investigation.initial_wrong_assumptions: Not documented in detail in sources consulted; do not speculate about early suspects
the_investigation.key_breakthrough: 2018 genetic genealogy pointing to the six sons of Jacquette and Albert Miller
the_investigation.the_fatal_mistake: Throwing away a coffee cup at the Tulalip Resort Casino in August 2018
the_investigation.how_long_until_caught: Arrest April 10, 2019: 46 years, 7 and a half months after the murder; verdict November 9, 2020: about 48 years and 2.5 months

the_confrontation._instructions: The arrest, raid, or climactic moment when everything collapses.
the_confrontation.scene_description: Detectives arrested Miller at his home; he was booked for first-degree murder with bail at $1 million
the_confrontation.protagonist_reaction: Pleaded not guilty; no confession documented
the_confrontation.ironic_or_absurd_details: He was 77, retired, running a ceramics shop with his wife; he had lived about five miles from the scene in 1972

legal_resolution.trial_date_if_applicable: October 2020 to November 9, 2020, Snohomish County Superior Court
legal_resolution.notable_court_testimony: Jana Loomis-Smith identified the boots she had lent her sister; the deposition of the man who found Jody (since deceased) was used; forensic scientists described the boot DNA and coffee cup match; the defense argued contamination

victim_impact_statements.key_quote: Paraphrase only: she did not want vengeance, she wanted the court record to say Miller murdered her sister; both parents died without knowing; she hoped the outcome would give hope to other families

legal_resolution.sentence_received: None: Miller died by suicide hours before the verdict; on December 18, 2020, Judge Kurtz upheld the conviction and signed a document affirming guilt beyond a reasonable doubt instead of sentencing
legal_resolution.current_status: Terrence Miller is dead (November 9, 2020). His first-degree murder conviction was upheld by the trial judge on December 18, 2020. No appeal or later change reported in sources found (as of October 2026). Case closed.
